## How to use this

The code from Lecture 16, filled in, with the numbers it produces.

. . .

Optimizers are numerical, so your last decimal place may differ from mine.
Anything beyond that is worth asking about.

::: {.notes}
Posted after class so nobody is left wondering whether their answer was right.
:::

## Setting up

```{r}
bbs <- read.csv("https://github.com/bmaitner/biometry_course/raw/refs/heads/main/data/BBS/FL_BBS.csv")

n_routes_by_year <- tapply(bbs$Route, bbs$Year, function(x){ length(unique(x)) })

bob_all <- bbs[bbs$Scientific_Name == "Colinus virginianus", ]
n_occ_by_year <- tapply(bob_all$Route, bob_all$Year, function(x){ length(unique(x)) })

occ <- data.frame(year = as.numeric(names(n_routes_by_year)),
                  n_routes = as.vector(n_routes_by_year),
                  n_occupied = as.vector(n_occ_by_year))

occ <- occ[occ$n_routes > 10, ]
occ$elapsed <- occ$year - min(occ$year)

c(rows = nrow(occ), first = min(occ$year), last = max(occ$year))
```

## The one-number answer {.smaller}

```{r}
const_nll <- function(p){
  -sum(dbinom(occ$n_occupied, size = occ$n_routes, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}

const_fit <- optimize(const_nll, interval = c(0, 1))

c(p = const_fit$minimum, nll = const_fit$objective)
```

Which is exactly the pooled proportion:

```{r}
sum(occ$n_occupied) / sum(occ$n_routes)
```

::: {.notes}
The number to beat was 79.91.
:::

## Why the straight line failed {.smaller}

The error was not your typing. At the starting values `a = 0.5` and `b = 0.05`,
the last year gives

```{r}
0.5 + 0.05 * 22
```

and a probability of 1.6 is not a probability:

```{r}
dbinom(52, size = 71, prob = 1.6, log = TRUE)
```

`optim()` cannot compare `NaN` with anything, so it stops before it starts. Any
unbounded line will eventually do this. That is what the logit fixes.

## Your turn 1: fitting the decline {.smaller}

The two pieces you had to supply were the **body** and the **call**:

```{r}
occ_nll <- function(a, b){
  p <- plogis(a + b * occ$elapsed)
  -sum(dbinom(occ$n_occupied, size = occ$n_routes, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}

fit_occ <- optim(par = c(a = 2, b = -0.05),
                 fn = function(p){
                   occ_nll(p["a"], p["b"])
                 },
                 method = "BFGS")

round(fit_occ$par, 4)
round(fit_occ$value, 2)
```

::: {.notes}
56.69 against 79.91, so 23 units for one extra parameter.
:::

## What those two numbers mean {.smaller}

```{r}
unname(plogis(fit_occ$par["a"]))                          # occupancy in 1997
unname(plogis(fit_occ$par["a"] + 22 * fit_occ$par["b"]))  # occupancy in 2019
unname(exp(fit_occ$par["b"]))                             # odds multiplier per year
```

`b` is a change in **log odds**, not in probability.

- 1997 odds: 0.88 / 0.12 = about 7.5 to 1
- multiply by 0.94, twenty-two times: `r round(7.5 * exp(fit_occ$par["b"])^22, 2)` to 1
- which is a probability of about 0.66

. . .

Reporting `b = -0.062` as "a 6% decline in occupancy" is the common mistake. It
is a 6% decline in the **odds**.

## Checking it by eye {.smaller}

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-width: 7
plot(occ$elapsed, occ$n_occupied / occ$n_routes, pch = 16,
     ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "years since 1997", ylab = "proportion occupied")

elapsed_seq <- 0:22

lines(elapsed_seq,
      plogis(fit_occ$par["a"] + fit_occ$par["b"] * elapsed_seq),
      col = "red", lwd = 3)
```

## The `mle2()` route, and `glm()` {.smaller}

```{r}
library(bbmle)

occ_nll2 <- function(params, n_occupied, n_routes, elapsed){
  p <- plogis(params[1] + params[2] * elapsed)
  -sum(dbinom(n_occupied, size = n_routes, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}

parnames(occ_nll2) <- c("a", "b")

m_occ <- mle2(minuslogl = occ_nll2,
              start = c(a = 2, b = -0.05),
              data = list(n_occupied = occ$n_occupied,
                          n_routes = occ$n_routes,
                          elapsed = occ$elapsed))

round(coef(m_occ), 4)

round(coef(glm(cbind(n_occupied, n_routes - n_occupied) ~ elapsed,
               data = occ, family = binomial)), 4)
```

Three routes, one answer.

## Your turn 2: the habitat effect {.smaller}

```{r}
y_bob <- bob_all$total_sightings
u_bob <- bob_all$frac_built

urban_nll <- function(mu0, b, size){
  mu <- mu0 * exp(b * u_bob)
  -sum(dnbinom(y_bob, mu = mu, size = size, log = TRUE))
}

fit_urban <- optim(par = c(mu0 = 12, b = -3, size = 1.4),
                   fn = function(p){
                     urban_nll(p["mu0"], p["b"], p["size"])
                   },
                   method = "L-BFGS-B",
                   lower = c(0.1, -20, 0.05),
                   upper = c(100, 20, 50))

round(fit_urban$par, 3)
round(fit_urban$value, 1)
```

## What the model expects {.smaller}

```{r}
mu0 <- fit_urban$par["mu0"]
b <- fit_urban$par["b"]

round(mu0 * exp(b * c(0, 0.05, 0.2, 0.5)), 2)      # 0%, 5%, 20%, 50% developed

round(unname(log(2) / abs(b)), 3)                 # development that halves the count
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.7
#| fig-width: 7
br <- cut(u_bob, breaks = c(0, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 1), include.lowest = TRUE)
mids <- c(0.01, 0.035, 0.075, 0.15, 0.3, 0.6)
plot(u_bob, y_bob, pch = 16, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.12), ylim = c(0, 40),
     xlab = "fraction developed", ylab = "bobwhite counted")
points(mids, tapply(y_bob, br, mean), pch = 17, cex = 1.5, col = "#2166ac")
uu <- seq(0, 0.5, length.out = 200)
lines(uu, mu0 * exp(b * uu), col = "red", lwd = 3)
```

Every 21 percentage points of development costs about half the birds.

## The three count models {.smaller}

```{r}
year_bob <- bob_all$Year - min(bob_all$Year)

flat <- optimize(function(s){
  -sum(dnbinom(y_bob, mu = mean(y_bob), size = s, log = TRUE))
}, interval = c(0.05, 50))

trend <- optim(par = c(mu0 = 15, decline = 0.03, size = 1),
               fn = function(p){
                 mu <- p["mu0"] * (1 - p["decline"])^year_bob
                 -sum(dnbinom(y_bob, mu = mu, size = p["size"], log = TRUE))
               },
               method = "L-BFGS-B",
               lower = c(0.1, -0.5, 0.05), upper = c(100, 0.5, 50))

round(c(flat = flat$objective, year = trend$value, development = fit_urban$value), 1)
```

Equal parameter counts for the last two, so the lower one simply wins.

. . .

But `frac_built` does not change over the 23 years, so it describes **where** the
birds are, not **why** they declined.

## Additional practice: reef richness {.smaller}

```{r}
reef <- read.csv("https://github.com/bmaitner/biometry_course/raw/refs/heads/main/data/Reef_fish/NCRMP_reef_fish_surveys.csv")

depth <- reef$DEPTH
rich <- reef$species_richness

var(rich) / mean(rich)        # overdispersed, so negative binomial
```

```{r}
reef_nll <- function(peak, opt, width, size){
  mu <- peak * exp(-(depth - opt)^2 / (2 * width^2))
  -sum(dnbinom(rich, mu = mu, size = size, log = TRUE))
}

fit_reef <- optim(par = c(peak = 25, opt = 20, width = 15, size = 10),
                  fn = function(p){
                    reef_nll(p["peak"], p["opt"], p["width"], p["size"])
                  },
                  method = "L-BFGS-B",
                  lower = c(1, 0, 1, 0.1), upper = c(200, 60, 200, 1000))

round(fit_reef$par, 2)
```

## Does the curve match the cloud? {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.9
#| fig-width: 7
plot(depth, rich, pch = 16, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.05),
     xlab = "depth (m)", ylab = "species richness")
dbr <- cut(depth, breaks = seq(0, 32.5, by = 2.5))
dmid <- seq(1.25, 31.25, by = 2.5)
points(dmid, tapply(rich, dbr, mean), pch = 17, cex = 1.4, col = "#2166ac")
dd <- seq(0, 32, length.out = 200)
lines(dd, fit_reef$par["peak"] *
        exp(-(dd - fit_reef$par["opt"])^2 / (2 * fit_reef$par["width"]^2)),
      col = "red", lwd = 3)
legend("topright", c("binned means", "fitted curve"), pch = c(17, NA),
       lty = c(NA, 1), lwd = c(NA, 3), col = c("#2166ac", "red"),
       bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

```{r}
flat_reef <- optimize(function(s){
  -sum(dnbinom(rich, mu = mean(rich), size = s, log = TRUE))
}, interval = c(0.1, 1000))

round(c(hump = fit_reef$value, flat = flat_reef$objective), 1)
```

An optimum near **`r round(fit_reef$par["opt"], 0)` m**, but a width of
**`r round(fit_reef$par["width"], 0)` m**: real, and very gentle.

## What to take away

1. A parameter can be a **function of a covariate**. Nothing else changes.
2. Constrained parameters get **transformed**, so the optimizer cannot wander
   anywhere illegal.
3. Interpret the estimate **on the scale you fitted it**: log odds, or logs.
4. **Check it**: against a second route to the same fit, and against a plot.

::: {.notes}
Point 3 is the one that produces wrong sentences in papers.
:::
